transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-27 15:00 PDT
Duration: 72 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood CSM), Marta Ruiz (HelixThera Head of Data), Devon Park (HelixThera Security), Ellen Cho (HelixThera ML), Liam O'Neill (HelixThera PM)

Auto-summary (auto):
- POC scoping to validate secure prompt handling, ephemeral vs persisted prompt storage, redaction fidelity, and throughput/latency benchmarks for HelixThera's triage assistant workload.
- Agreement to exchange benchmark artifacts and sample prompts; Redwood to propose runner and test matrix.
- Next: share scripts, security docs, schedule private VPC pilot.

Topics: PII classification, ephemeral logs, retention windows, KMS integration, throughput sizing, canary rollouts

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone thanks for joining. we're gonna run through the poc scope for the prompt handling and benchmarks. I see all attendees, shout out if I'm missing someone.
[00:10] Marta Ruiz: Hi Jordan, thanks. good to be here. quick context — we have a product team building a clinical triage assistant, a lot of sensitive patient content flows through prompts. Our main concerns are: no persistent storage of raw prompts unless specifically permitted, must support redaction of PHI before logs are stored, and we need predictable latency under 300ms p50 for short prompts.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: Got it. Priya do you want to walk through the technical approach we usually recommend?
[00:35] Priya Kapoor: Sure. so high level for this PoC we propose two tracks: 1) security/handling: ensure PII/PHI is either ephemerally handled or redacted before any persistent logs; and 2) performance: run the throughput and tail latency benchmarks against a workload that matches HelixThera's traffic profile.
[00:55] Devon Park: When you say ephemeral — do you mean never write prompts to disk, or write encrypted and then purge? we have restrictions from compliance that logs older than 24 hours must be deleted unless flagged.
[01:10] Priya Kapoor: Good question. Redwood supports an ephemeral mode where by default prompt content is kept in memory and not written to persistent storage unless you enable prompt archiving. For private deployment, you can opt into in-transit encryption and envelope encryption with your KMS so anything written is customer-managed keys. Also we can configure a TTL for logs and an automated redaction hook before they hit storage.
[01:33] Devon Park: OK that helps. Are redaction hooks server-side? Like do you run a pattern-based sanitizer or an ML redactor?
[01:40] Priya Kapoor: We support multiple approaches. Out of the box you can use pattern and rule-based redaction (regex for SSNs, PHI tokens) and we also have an ML redaction model for fuzzy PII detection. For the PoC we recommend a hybrid: quick rule-based passes for obvious patterns, then an ML pass that flags potential PHI for review. You can choose to persist the flags (metadata) while the actual prompt text is removed.
[02:05] Ellen Cho: For our workflows, we are worried about false positives from ML redaction causing loss of signal. Can the redaction be lossy but reversible for internal debugging under strict audit?
[02:15] Priya Kapoor: You can store a cryptographic hash of the redacted spans and map back if needed, but we recommend against storing plain text. For debugging in the PoC we can enable a time-limited debug mode where redacted content is stored in an audit bucket for 72 hours and access is audited and gated by RBAC.
[02:32] Liam O'Neill: Is that debug bucket under our control in a private deployment? We need that for SOC2 auditors.
[02:38] Samir Patel: Yes, for Private/VPC deployments the audit bucket and KMS are under the customer's cloud account and keys, so HelixThera controls retention and access. For Hosted customers we offer managed keys but you can also bring-your-own-key (BYOK).
[02:55] Marta Ruiz: Timeline wise, we're targeting a decision by end of May and a 2-week internal pilot in June. Is that realistic?
[03:03] Jordan Lee: Totally feasible. My proposal: Redwood delivers benchmark plan and runner by next week, you provide sample prompts and traffic profile, then we schedule the benchmark run and security review. If the private VPC option is needed we'll run that in the second week.
[03:20] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. On benchmarks, we need p50/p95 latencies and per-token cost estimation. Also want to include degraded-mode behavior — what happens when large models are overloaded.
[03:33] Priya Kapoor: We'll include: steady-state throughput (req/s), latency distributions with warm/cold cache, token-cost estimates for quantized and unquantized variants, and an overload/fallback test where requests route to a cheaper variant if the primary model is saturated. We'll also capture KV cache hit-rates since your triage flows reuse context heavily.
[03:53] Devon Park: About KV cache and telemetry: Do you log KV cache entries? We can't keep any user identifiers in cache persistence.
[03:59] Priya Kapoor: Cache entries are by default ephemeral in memory and not persisted to disk unless you enable persistent checkpointing. For PoC we'll keep everything in-memory and scrub identifiers from cache keys; we can also namespace caches per tenant so even if something persists it's isolated.
[04:18] Ellen Cho: For the benchmark workload, our traffic is bursty — avg 1200 reqs/hour, peak 350 rps during clinical hours, average prompt length 80 tokens, response 150 tokens. Can you size the GPU pool for that?
[04:31] Priya Kapoor: Yes — we'll model steady and peak. For a hosted run we'll provision an autoscaling pool to reach your peak with an SLO on p95. For a private deployment we'll give guidance: e.g., for model X (7B quantized) with batching and KV cache, you'd need N GPUs; we'll itemize in the benchmark plan.
[04:48] Jordan Lee: Quick note: since HelixThera needs low latency, we recommend prioritizing lower-sequence-length optimizations and prefix caching so repeated clinical context doesn't re-tokenize. That reduces cost and latency.
[05:00] Liam O'Neill: On retention settings, we need a matrix: what gets kept immediately, what gets kept hashed, what gets purged after TTL. Can you prepare a suggested retention matrix?
[05:10] Samir Patel: We'll draft a retention matrix that maps data class (raw prompt, redacted prompt, runtime metadata, model outputs, traces) to default TTLs and options for encryption in transit/at rest. We'll flag items that require customer sign-off for retention >24 hours.
[05:22] Marta Ruiz: Also auditors will want to see access logs and a chain of custody for any stored prompt text. Can Redwood provide detailed audit logs with SAML assertions and user identifiers?
[05:31] Samir Patel: Yes, audit logs include user id, action, resource, timestamp, and can be forwarded to your SIEM. For private deploy we can integrate with your SAML SSO and push logs directly to your cloud logging.
[05:44] Devon Park: A couple of nitty gritty questions: are model weights ever written to disk in the host? and what about swap/eviction that might land on disk?
[05:54] Priya Kapoor: In our runtime, model weights are loaded into GPU memory and may have disk-backed checkpoints if you enable persistence. For the PoC we'll disable persistence and ensure no swap to disk via memory locking; we'll share our hardening checklist and runtime flags.
[06:08] Ellen Cho: For redaction tests, can you run a set of 200 synthetic prompts with intentionally embedded PHI variants and show false positive/negative rates?
[06:16] Priya Kapoor: Absolutely — we'll run a redaction accuracy test and report precision/recall. We'll also show how rule-based filters and ML redactor combine to catch edge cases.
[06:25] Marta Ruiz: Pricing — I know this is early, but can you provide estimated token cost differences between hosted quantized and private dedicated?
[06:33] Jordan Lee: We'll include cost estimates in the benchmark report. Roughly, quantized hosted runs tend to be cheaper on per-token basis, but private dedicated can be better if you have sustained high throughput because of reserved capacity discounts. We'll put example calculations for your expected monthly volume.
[06:48] Liam O'Neill: Are there any legal gating items we should surface now for the pilot? subprocessors? data residency?
[06:55] Samir Patel: For hosted we use cloud providers as subprocessors; we can provide a subprocessors list and data residency options. For customers with strict requirements, private on-prem or VPC with BYOK removes most concerns. We'll provide our SOC2 report and ISO certs for review.
[07:08] Devon Park: One more: can we opt for ephemeral prompt references where only a salted hash is stored so we can link events without storing content?
[07:16] Priya Kapoor: Yes, hashed references are supported and we can show an implementation pattern. We'll include sample code for generating salted hashes and how to map them to audit events.
[07:26] Jordan Lee: Ok let's talk logistics for the benchmark run. Priya will own the runner and test matrix. We'll need Ellen's sample prompts, Marta to confirm success criteria, and Devon to sign off on security config. After the run we'll do a 1-hour deep-dive to review results.
[07:42] Marta Ruiz: Success criteria from our side: 1) redaction recall >= 98% on our test set, 2) p95 latency <= 500ms on peak simulation (we can accept p50 < 250ms), 3) no raw prompt persisted beyond 24 hours unless explicitly archived with encryption and audit.
[07:58] Priya Kapoor: Noted. We'll align metrics. Also propose an acceptance threshold for fallback correctness — when a request is downscaled to cheaper model, response quality should remain above a BLEU-style or domain-specific score we define together.
[08:12] Ellen Cho: We'll produce a small eval set and quality rubric. I can get that over by Friday.
[08:17] Jordan Lee: Perfect. Any blockers to running an initial hosted benchmark next week?
[08:21] Liam O'Neill: Need legal to ok a minimal NDA for sharing sample prompts, but that's in process.
[08:26] Samir Patel: We'll send a short PoC agreement template plus a security addendum for sample sharing.
[08:31] Marta Ruiz: Great. A few random notes I heard — can you also include how you handle function/tool calling traces and whether those traces contain prompt text?
[08:40] Priya Kapoor: Function traces can be configured. By default we don't persist full prompt bodies in function traces. You can emit structured arguments only, or store masked invocation payloads. We'll include examples.
[08:50] Devon Park: Also, for onboarding, do you provide a runbook for incident response if prompt leakage is detected?
[08:57] Samir Patel: Yes — we'll include an incident response playbook, notification windows, and remediation steps.
[09:03] Jordan Lee: Ok we'll wrap up with a recap.
[09:05] Jordan Lee: Recap: Redwood to share benchmark plan + runner script, sample retention matrix, security checklist, and PoC agreement. HelixThera to share sample prompts, evaluation rubric, and security contact sign-off. Schedule bench run week of 2026-05-11 for private VPC if requested.
[09:24] Marta Ruiz: Thanks everyone.
[09:26] Liam O'Neill: Thanks.
[09:27] Ellen Cho: bye
[09:28] Devon Park: thanks

End of transcript.
